content: Floaters are small, shadowy shapes that appear in your field of vision. They may resemble spots, thread-like strands, or squiggly lines. These floaters are tiny fragments of cellular debris that drift within the vitreous humor of the eye and typically do not require treatment as they often come and go on their own. Symptoms of Floaters Individuals with floaters often notice small specks or cobwebs that seem to float across their vision. These are particularly noticeable when looking at bright backgrounds, such as a white piece of paper or a clear blue sky. Floaters tend to move as the eyes move and may dart away when one tries to focus on them directly. They do not precisely follow eye movements and usually drift when the eyes stop moving. While most people have floaters and learn to ignore them, they may become more noticeable or bothersome if they increase in number or prominence. Causes of Floaters Floaters occur when the vitreous humor, a gel-like substance that fills approximately 80% of the eye and helps maintain its round shape, begins to shrink with age. As the vitreous shrinks, it can develop stringy structures that cast tiny shadows on the retina, which are perceived as floaters. However, floaters can also result from more serious conditions, such as infections, inflammation (uveitis), bleeding, retinal tears, or trauma to the eye. Risk Factors The likelihood of developing floaters increases with age. They are more common in individuals who are highly nearsighted, have diabetes, or have undergone cataract surgery. Diagnosis of Floaters Floaters can often be observed by an ophthalmologist or optometrist using specialized tools such as an ophthalmoscope or slit lamp. However, if the floater is a small piece of debris located near the retina, it may not be visible to the examiner, even if it appears large to the patient. Techniques such as increasing background illumination or using a pinhole to reduce pupil size may help individuals better visualize their own floaters. Tilting the head to allow a floater to drift toward the central axis of the eye can also make its fibrous elements more apparent. A meta-analysis published in the Journal of the American Medical Association reported that the presence of retinal tears in patients with new-onset floaters was surprisingly high, at 14% (95% confidence interval: 12%-16%). Patients experiencing new floaters, especially when accompanied by flashes of light, visual loss, or visual field restriction, should seek urgent ophthalmologic evaluation. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care A small number of floaters are a normal part of aging and are not considered a medical emergency. However, a sudden increase in floaters, particularly if accompanied by flashes of light or peripheral vision loss, may indicate a retinal detachment. Retinal detachment occurs when part of the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye, is lifted or pulled from its normal position. This is a serious condition and should always be treated as an emergency. If left untreated, retinal detachment can lead to permanent visual impairment within two to three days or even blindness in the affected eye. Individuals experiencing these symptoms should consult an eye care professional immediately. Treatment Options For most people, floaters are simply an annoyance and do not require treatment. However, in rare cases, floaters can become so dense and numerous that they significantly impair vision. In such instances, a surgical procedure called a vitrectomy may be necessary. A vitrectomy involves removing the vitreous gel, along with its floating debris, from the eye and replacing it with a saline solution. Since the vitreous is mostly water, patients typically do not notice any difference between the saline solution and the original vitreous. However, this surgery carries significant risks, including retinal detachment, retinal tears, and cataract formation. As a result, most eye surgeons are reluctant to recommend this procedure unless the floaters severely interfere with vision. Prevention of Floaters Floaters cannot be prevented. However, seeking prompt medical attention for symptoms of retinal tears or retinal detachment can help prevent vision loss. Prognosis In most cases, floaters are a natural part of the aging process and are more of a nuisance than a serious medical issue. While they may initially be distracting, they often settle at the bottom of the eye over time, becoming less bothersome. However, they do not disappear completely. Occasionally, a section of the vitreous may pull away from the retina all at once, rather than gradually, causing a sudden appearance of many new floaters. This condition, known as vitreous detachment, is usually not sight-threatening and does not require treatment. Nevertheless, a sudden increase in floaters, especially if accompanied by flashes of light or peripheral vision loss, could indicate a retinal detachment. If left untreated, retinal detachment can result in permanent visual impairment or blindness within a few days. Immediate medical attention is essential in such cases.
